article.title: UCL-Led Excavation Near Chelmsford Uncovers Iron Age Cemetery With High-Status Burials Predating the Roman Conquest
article.summary: Archaeology South-East's excavation near Chelmsford has revealed a 2,000-year-old cemetery of over 100 cremation burials, including five richly furnished graves pointing to pre-conquest ties with Rome.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

Archaeologists from Archaeology South-East, part of the UCL Institute of Archaeology, have completed excavations near Chelmsford, Essex, uncovering a cemetery holding the cremated remains of over 100 individuals dating from around 2,000 years ago, according to [UCL](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2026/jul/high-status-iron-age-burials-reveal-early-links-roman-empire). The burials sit inside a square-shaped, ditched enclosure mostly dating to the first century AD, spanning the transition to Roman rule in Britain that followed Emperor Claudius' invasion in AD 43, as [UCL](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2026/jul/high-status-iron-age-burials-reveal-early-links-roman-empire) and [Phys.org](https://phys.org/news/2026-07-high-status-iron-age-burials.html) report.

## Five Richly Furnished Graves

Among dozens of simpler cremation burials contained in urns, excavators identified five richly furnished, high-status cremation burials, according to [Arkeonews](https://arkeonews.net/2000-year-old-cemetery-with-lavishly-adorned-elite-burials-uncovered-in-england/). In these graves, the human remains were distinct from the surrounding burials: piles of burnt bone deposited within large, square pits and surrounded by collections of objects, both functional and rare, that indicated the owner's importance in Iron Age East Anglia, according to [UCL](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2026/jul/high-status-iron-age-burials-reveal-early-links-roman-empire). The grave goods recovered from these burials include copper alloy vessels, ceramic wine jars known as amphorae, a pillar-moulded glass bowl, hobnails, and brooches, all of which are now being cleaned, conserved, and analyzed by specialist teams at Archaeology South-East, per [UCL](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2026/jul/high-status-iron-age-burials-reveal-early-links-roman-empire).

Angus Forshaw, who led the excavation for Archaeology South-East, said the finds point to contact between Iron Age Britain and Rome that predates the conquest: "These exceptional grave goods are likely a reflection of diplomatic contact and economic exchange between Iron Age people in Britain and the Roman Empire, which was happening prior to the Roman conquest of AD43," according to [UCL](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2026/jul/high-status-iron-age-burials-reveal-early-links-roman-empire). Forshaw added: "The pillar-moulded glass bowl alone – one of the earliest glass vessels to arrive in Britain – would have been a highly-prized personal possession, and the amphorae could have arrived in Britain filled with wine, intended for consumption by society's elites," per [UCL](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2026/jul/high-status-iron-age-burials-reveal-early-links-roman-empire).

Samara King, project manager at Archaeology South-East, framed the burials as a form of social signaling during a period of upheaval: "The period around the Roman conquest was a time of immense political and cultural change. These burials may have been a way in which different Iron Age communities signalled their identities, their power, and perceived allegiance to Rome," according to [UCL](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2026/jul/high-status-iron-age-burials-reveal-early-links-roman-empire).

## A Wider Iron Age Landscape

The cemetery was not an isolated find. Excavations across 11 hectares revealed at least three previously unknown Iron Age settlements made up of multiple roundhouses enclosed by ditches, with associated field systems, waterholes, and smaller agricultural enclosures, according to [UCL](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2026/jul/high-status-iron-age-burials-reveal-early-links-roman-empire). Initial research suggests the high-status burials are similar to other finds in the region, reminiscent of cremations uncovered at Stansted and Stanway, as well as at sites in Hertfordshire known as Welwyn-type burials, per [UCL](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2026/jul/high-status-iron-age-burials-reveal-early-links-roman-empire). Researchers are continuing to analyze the material from the burials, hoping further dating work will clarify how the cemetery relates to the nearby settlements and help identify who the high-status individuals might have been, [UCL](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2026/jul/high-status-iron-age-burials-reveal-early-links-roman-empire) reports.

## Public Display and Local Context

Ten of the excavated objects, including glassware, amphorae, and other ceramic items, will go on public display at the Museum of Chelmsford in a new exhibition, *Timeless Treasures: Unlocking the Great Baddow Coin Hoard*, which opened on Saturday, July 18, and runs until April 11, 2027, according to [UCL](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2026/jul/high-status-iron-age-burials-reveal-early-links-roman-empire) and [Chelmsford City Council](https://citylife.chelmsford.gov.uk/posts/high-status-iron-age-burials-discovered-in-chelmsford-reveal-early-links-to-roman-empire). The exhibition places the newly discovered cemetery alongside the Great Baddow Hoard, a cache of 935 Iron Age gold coins discovered in a field in Great Baddow, Chelmsford, in 2020, according to [UCL](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2026/jul/high-status-iron-age-burials-reveal-early-links-roman-empire). A separate UCL account of the hoard's cataloguing notes the total comprises 933 originally recorded coins plus two additional coins recovered during more recent excavation work, according to [UCL Faculty of Social & Historical Sciences](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/social-historical-sciences/news/2026/may/chelmsford-excavation-uncovers-two-further-coins-late-iron-age-hoard).

Claire Willetts, Curator and Exhibitions Officer at the Museum of Chelmsford, said the two discoveries together reframe the town's ancient history: "Coupled with the discovery of the Great Baddow Hoard, this newly uncovered Iron Age cemetery and the finds within it demonstrate that Chelmsford was not a quiet backwater during the Iron Age – it was part of a busy and connected landscape. Could the Great Baddow Hoard have links to this cemetery? We'll explore this and other theories in our new exhibit," according to [UCL](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2026/jul/high-status-iron-age-burials-reveal-early-links-roman-empire). A public talk with Forshaw at the Museum of Chelmsford, further exploring what the graves reveal about elite society in Late Iron Age and Roman Essex, is planned for later this year, per [UCL](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2026/jul/high-status-iron-age-burials-reveal-early-links-roman-empire).

## What We Don't Know

The identities of the high-status individuals buried in the cemetery remain unknown, and researchers say further dating and analysis of the recovered material will be needed to determine how long the cemetery was in use and how it relates chronologically to the surrounding settlements, according to [UCL](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2026/jul/high-status-iron-age-burials-reveal-early-links-roman-empire). Whether the cemetery has any direct connection to the nearby Great Baddow coin hoard is, for now, a question the Museum of Chelmsford's new exhibition raises rather than answers, per [Chelmsford City Council](https://citylife.chelmsford.gov.uk/posts/high-status-iron-age-burials-discovered-in-chelmsford-reveal-early-links-to-roman-empire).
